Kettlebell Turkish Get Up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeGetting from lying to standing with a weight overhead trains shoulder stability, hip mobility and body control in one slow movement. It takes about half a minute per repetition, and it exposes every weak link you have.

  1. Lie on your back and press the bell overhead with one arm, that knee bent
  2. Roll onto the opposite forearm, then push up onto that hand
  3. Lift your hips and sweep the straight leg back into a kneeling position
  4. Bring your torso upright, then stand up, keeping the bell locked overhead throughout
  5. Reverse every step exactly to return to lying, then change arms
ea_kettlebell_turkish_get_up

Kettlebell Walkover Pushup

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeMoving a hand onto and off a kettlebell between push-ups adds a shoulder-stability and anti-rotation demand to a familiar movement. It also increases the depth on one side each repetition.

  1. Set a kettlebell on the floor and take a push-up position with one hand on it
  2. Keep your feet wide and your body in a straight line
  3. Lower into a push-up, then press back up
  4. Walk the free hand over the bell and swap which hand is on it
  5. Do another push-up and continue, alternating hands each repetition
ea_kettlebell_walkover_pushup

Kettlebell Windmill

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeHolding a weight overhead while bending sideways to the floor demands shoulder stability, hip mobility and trunk strength together. Start with no weight at all — the position is the hard part, not the load.

  1. Press a kettlebell overhead with one arm and turn both feet away from that side
  2. Keep your eyes on the bell and your arm straight, without forcing the elbow
  3. Push your hips toward the loaded side and slide the free hand down your leg
  4. Lower until that hand reaches the floor or as far as you can control with a neutral spine
  5. Return to standing along the same path, then finish the set and change sides
ea_kettlebell_windmill

Kipping Handstand Push-up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeUses a knee drive to help the arms press, which allows far more repetitions than a strict handstand push-up. It trains conditioning and rhythm, not raw pressing strength — learn the strict version first.

  1. Kick up into a handstand with your heels resting against a wall
  2. Lower under control until the top of your head touches the floor or a pad
  3. Tuck your knees toward your chest
  4. Drive the knees up hard and press with the arms at the same moment
  5. Lock out overhead, reset your body line, and repeat
ea_kipping_handstand_push_up elbowneckshoulderwrist

Landmine Alternating Lunge and Twist

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeCombines a lunge with a rotation, so the legs work while the trunk turns under load. It trains the two things together, which is how the body actually moves outside a gym.

  1. Hold the loaded bar end at chest height with both hands, standing away from the anchor
  2. Step back into a reverse lunge with one leg
  3. As you lower, rotate your ribs toward the front leg
  4. Untwist as you drive through the whole front foot to stand, keeping the heel grounded
  5. Repeat on the other leg, alternating throughout the set
ea_landmine_alternating_lunge_and_twist hipkneewrist

Landmine Alternating Lunge to Chest Press

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeA lunge that finishes as a press, so the legs and the upper body are trained in one continuous movement. The heart rate rises quickly, which makes it a conditioning exercise as much as a strength one.

  1. Hold the loaded bar end at one shoulder, facing away from the anchor
  2. Step back into a reverse lunge until the back knee is near the floor
  3. Drive through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to stand back up
  4. Press the bar forward and up to a straight arm as you finish standing
  5. Return it to the shoulder, switch sides, and repeat
ea_landmine_alternating_lunge_to_chest_press hipkneeshoulder

Landmine Rotational Lift to Press

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTakes the bar from low on one side to overhead on the other, which trains the diagonal chain from the hip through the trunk to the shoulder. That chain is what produces force in throwing and striking.

  1. Stand side-on to the landmine and hold the loaded end low beside one hip
  2. Bend your knees slightly and brace your stomach
  3. Rotate and drive up through the hips, lifting the bar diagonally across your body
  4. Finish by pressing it overhead on the opposite side
  5. Reverse the path under control, then complete the set and change sides
ea_landmine_rotational_lift_to_press kneeshoulder

Lateral Sled Drag

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeDragging sideways loads the side of the hip, which almost no other loaded exercise reaches. That muscle is what keeps the knee tracking properly, and it is chronically undertrained.

  1. Attach a strap to the sled and hold it with both hands
  2. Stand side-on to the sled with your knees bent and chest up
  3. Keep your feet pointing forward, not toward the sled
  4. Step sideways with the lead foot and follow with the other, pulling the sled along
  5. Cover the set distance, then turn around and lead with the other side
ea_lateral_sled_drag

Low Box Lateral Runner

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeQuick sideways steps on and off a low box train the feet and the side of the hip to react fast. It raises the heart rate quickly and needs almost no space.

  1. Stand side-on beside a low box with your knees bent
  2. Step the near foot onto the box, then the other foot
  3. Step down on the far side, one foot at a time, without pausing
  4. Reverse immediately and travel back the other way
  5. Keep the contacts light and quick for the set time
ea_low_box_lateral_runner

Low Box Quick Feet

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeTapping the box as fast as possible trains pure foot speed and the ability to change contact quickly. It is short, simple, and one of the best things to do at the end of a warm-up.

  1. Stand facing a low box with your knees slightly bent
  2. Tap the top of the box with the ball of one foot
  3. Swap feet as fast as you can, alternating taps
  4. Stay on the balls of your feet and keep your chest up
  5. Work for fifteen to twenty seconds, then rest and repeat
ea_low_box_quick_feet

Low Rotational Med Ball Chops (quarter Squat, Rotating Med Ball Left and Ride Across Core)

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeRotating a ball across the body from a quarter squat trains the trunk to turn while the legs hold a position. That combination is what every throwing and striking movement is built on.

  1. Hold a medicine ball with both hands and sink into a quarter squat
  2. Keep your chest up and your stomach braced
  3. Sweep the ball across your body from one hip toward the opposite shoulder
  4. Let your feet pivot slightly but keep the squat depth constant
  5. Control it back across and repeat, then work the other direction
ea_low_rotational_med_ball_chops_quarter_squat_rotating_med_ball_left_and_ride_across_core anklehipknee

Low Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposePushing from the low handles puts you in a more horizontal position, which shifts the work further onto the legs and makes it closer to a sprint start. Brutal on the quadriceps, with less landing impact than sprinting since there's no flight phase -- though the joints are still working hard under load.

  1. Load the sled and grip the low handles with straight arms
  2. Get your body as close to horizontal as you can while keeping your spine neutral
  3. Set your feet behind you and brace your stomach
  4. Drive forward with short, hard steps through the balls of your feet
  5. Push for the set distance, then rest fully before the next effort
ea_low_sled_push

Lying Neck Curls

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeStrengthens the front of the neck -- useful for anyone in a contact sport, and specialized work if you want to train the neck directly. Start with no weight at all and add it very slowly.

  1. Lie face up on a bench with your head and neck extending past the end
  2. Support your head at first, or place a folded towel under it
  3. Let your head lower back slowly until you feel a gentle stretch
  4. Curl your chin toward your chest, lifting the head under control
  5. Move slowly through a small range and stop well before any discomfort, especially anything sharp, radiating or numb
ea_lying_neck_curls elbowneckwrist

Lying Neck Extension

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeStrengthens the back of the neck -- specialized work for people who want to train the neck directly. Like all neck work, it needs very light loads and very slow movement.

  1. Lie face down on a bench with your head extending past the end
  2. Rest your arms comfortably and keep your shoulders relaxed
  3. Lower your chin toward your chest under control
  4. Lift your head back until it is level with your spine — no further
  5. Move slowly, never forcing, and stop at the first sign of discomfort, especially anything sharp, radiating or numb
ea_lying_neck_extension kneeneckwrist

Lying on Side Arm Circle Warm Up

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeLying on your side removes the compensation you get standing, so the shoulder has to move through its own range rather than borrowing from the back. It shows exactly where the movement runs out.

  1. Lie on one side with your knees bent and both arms out in front of you
  2. Keep the lower arm still and rest your head on it
  3. Sweep the top arm slowly in a large circle over your head and behind you
  4. Keep the hand as close to the floor as your shoulder allows
  5. Complete the circle back to the start and repeat, then change sides
ea_lying_on_side_arm_circle_warm_up

Major Groups Muscle Body

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose Revised

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand tall with your spine neutral, arms by your side, and feet shoulder-width apart
ea_major_groups_muscle_body

Med Ball Jumping Jacks

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeAdds a load to a familiar warm-up movement, which raises the heart rate faster and asks more of the shoulders. Useful as a bridge between a light warm-up and real work.

  1. Stand with feet together holding a medicine ball at your chest
  2. Jump the feet apart and press the ball overhead at the same time
  3. Land softly with the knees slightly bent
  4. Jump the feet back together and bring the ball to your chest
  5. Continue at a steady rhythm for the set time
ea_med_ball_jumping_jacks ankleknee

Med Ball Side Wall Slams

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThrowing sideways into a wall at full speed trains rotational power, which is what a golf swing, a punch and a throw all depend on. There is no way to train this slowly and get the same result.

  1. Stand side-on to a solid wall about a metre away, holding a medicine ball
  2. Set your feet shoulder width apart and take the ball to the far hip
  3. Rotate hard toward the wall, pivoting the back foot
  4. Throw the ball into the wall as forcefully as you can
  5. Catch the rebound, reset to the far hip, and repeat before changing sides
ea_med_ball_side_wall_slams

Med Ball Slam Burpees

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeChains a slam onto a burpee, which can raise the heart rate very quickly. Best used in short intervals — the point is intensity, not accumulating repetitions.

  1. Stand holding a medicine ball, feet shoulder width apart
  2. Raise it overhead and slam it into the floor with full force
  3. Place your hands on the ball or floor, jump your feet back into a plank
  4. Jump your feet back in and stand up, picking the ball up as you rise
  5. Go straight into the next slam and continue for the set
ea_med_ball_slam_burpees anklekneewrist

Monkey Bar Swings

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeSwinging hand over hand builds grip endurance and shoulder strength through a full overhead range, and it is one of the few upper-body exercises that is genuinely fun. Grip usually gives out first.

  1. Reach up and take hold of the first bar with an overhand grip
  2. Hang with your shoulders engaged, not slack
  3. Build a small swing with your legs and release one hand at the forward point
  4. Catch the next bar and let the swing carry you to the following one
  5. Continue the length of the bars, then drop down under control
ea_monkey_bar_swings hiplower_back

Mountain Climber Jumps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeSwitching both feet in the air at once turns a mountain climber into a jump, which raises both the heart rate and the demand on the stomach. Keep the hips low — that is what stops it becoming a shuffle.

  1. Start in a high plank with your hands under your shoulders
  2. Bring one foot forward beside your hand, the other leg straight back
  3. Jump and switch both feet in the air at the same time
  4. Land softly with the hips staying low and the spine neutral
  5. Keep switching at a steady pace for the set time
ea_mountain_climber_jumps anklekneewrist

Overhead Med Ball Throw

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThrowing overhead for distance trains the whole body to extend explosively, from the ankles through the hips to the arms. It is one of the simplest ways to measure and train full-body power.

  1. Stand facing an open space or a wall, holding a medicine ball at your chest
  2. Raise it overhead and let your body extend slightly backwards
  3. Brace your stomach so the movement does not come from the lower back
  4. Throw the ball forward and up with everything you have
  5. Retrieve it, reset your position, and repeat
ea_overhead_med_ball_throw shoulder

Pike Alternating Opposite Hip Taps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeReaching for the opposite hip from a pike position forces one shoulder to hold your whole weight while the trunk resists rotating. It builds the shoulder stability that overhead work needs.

  1. Start in a high plank and walk your feet in so your hips lift into a pike
  2. Keep your legs as straight as you can and your head between your arms
  3. Shift your weight onto one hand
  4. Reach the other hand back to tap the opposite hip, keeping the hips square
  5. Return it to the floor and alternate for the set
ea_pike_alternating_opposite_hip_taps shoulder

Pike Individual Alternating Arm Reaches

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeReaching one arm forward from a pike loads the supporting shoulder heavily while asking it to stay stable. It is a step on the way to a handstand, and useful long before you get there.

  1. Set up in a pike position with the hips high and the head between the arms
  2. Push the floor away and keep the shoulders active
  3. Shift your weight onto one hand and lift the other off the floor
  4. Reach it forward along the floor without letting the hips twist
  5. Return it and alternate arms for the set
ea_pike_individual_alternating_arm_reaches shoulder

Pike Jacks Feet Kicking in and Out

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeJumping the feet in and out from a pike keeps the shoulders under load while the legs work, which makes it a conditioning drill and a shoulder exercise at once.

  1. Start in a pike position with your hips high and hands under your shoulders
  2. Keep your arms straight and your head between them
  3. Jump both feet apart, then jump them back together
  4. Keep the hips high throughout — do not let them drop toward a plank
  5. Continue at a steady rhythm for the set time
ea_pike_jacks_feet_kicking_in_and_out anklekneeshoulder

Pike Shoulder Taps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe simplest of the pike drills and the place to start: tapping the opposite shoulder loads one arm at a time while the trunk stops the hips rotating. Good preparation for handstand work.

  1. Walk your feet toward your hands from a plank until your hips are high
  2. Keep your arms straight and your head between your upper arms
  3. Shift your weight onto one hand
  4. Tap the opposite shoulder with the free hand, keeping the hips level
  5. Replace the hand and alternate sides for the set
ea_pike_shoulder_taps shoulder

Plank IYTW

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeFour arm positions in one set, each reaching a different part of the upper back and shoulder. It is a warm-up and a posture exercise combined, and the light weight is deliberate.

  1. Set up in a plank with a light dumbbell in each hand, feet wide
  2. Lift one arm straight forward past your head to make an I, then lower
  3. Raise it out at a diagonal to make a Y, then lower
  4. Take it straight out to the side for a T, then bend the elbow back for a W
  5. Repeat the whole sequence on the other arm, keeping the hips completely still
ea_plank_iytw elbowwrist

Plank Individual Arm Reach

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeLifting one hand from a plank halves your base of support, so the stomach has to work much harder to stop the hips rotating. Far more effective than simply holding a plank for longer.

  1. Start in a plank on your hands or forearms with the feet wide
  2. Squeeze your glutes and stomach so your body is one straight line
  3. Shift your weight slightly and lift one hand off the floor
  4. Reach it straight forward, keeping both hips level with the floor
  5. Return it and alternate arms, moving slowly throughout
ea_plank_individual_arm_reach elbowwrist

Plank Lunges

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Begin in a plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels
  2. Bring your right knee forward and place your right foot outside your right hand, keeping your left leg extended straight back
  3. Return your right foot to the plank position
  4. Repeat the movement with your left knee, bringing your left foot forward to place it outside your left hand. Alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions
ea_plank_lunges elbowhipkneelower_backwrist

Plank Pushup

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeMoving between forearms and hands trains the shoulders to press while the trunk holds a rigid line. It is harder than either a plank or a push-up alone, and needs nothing at all.

  1. Start in a forearm plank with your elbows under your shoulders
  2. Squeeze your glutes and keep your body in one straight line
  3. Press up onto one hand, then the other, until your arms are straight
  4. Lower back down one forearm at a time in the same order
  5. Alternate which arm leads and continue for the set
ea_plank_pushup elbowwrist

Plank Shoulder Taps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Begin in a plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels
  2. Lift your right hand off the floor and tap your left shoulder, keeping your hips stable and minimizing rotation
  3. Return your right hand to the starting position
  4. Repeat the movement with your left hand, lifting it off the floor and tapping your right shoulder. Alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions
ea_plank_shoulder_taps elbowwrist

Plate Overhead Carry

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeWalking with a weight locked overhead demands that the shoulders stay stable and the ribs stay down for the whole distance. It exposes a weak brace faster than almost any other exercise.

  1. Press a plate overhead with straight arms, directly above your shoulders
  2. Pull your ribs down and squeeze your glutes
  3. Keep your head neutral and look straight ahead
  4. Walk in a straight line with controlled steps, arms locked
  5. Cover the set distance, then lower the plate under control
ea_plate_overhead_carry shoulder

Pull Sled or Dog Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeLoaded walking with no lowering phase, which trains the legs and the heart hard while often costing much less in recovery than exercises with a lowering phase. That combination is why sleds appear in nearly every serious training programme.

  1. Attach a harness or hold the straps and take up the slack
  2. Lean into the load with your arms firm and your spine neutral
  3. Set your feet behind your hips and brace your stomach
  4. Drive forward with short, deliberate steps at a steady pace
  5. Cover the set distance, then rest before the next effort
ea_pull_sled_or_dog_sled_push

Pushup to Renegade Row

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeA push and a pull in the same repetition, with the stomach working the whole time to stop the hips rotating. One of the most efficient upper-body exercises there is when time is short.

  1. Take a push-up position gripping a dumbbell in each hand, feet wide
  2. Lower into a push-up and press back up
  3. Shift your weight to one side and row the opposite dumbbell to your ribs
  4. Keep both hips square to the floor as you row — this is the hard part
  5. Lower it, do another push-up, and row the other side
ea_pushup_to_renegade_row upper_back

Rebounder High Knee Runs

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeRunning on a trampoline gives much of the cardiovascular work of running with noticeably less impact through the knees and shins than running on hard ground. It can be a useful option if joints feel mildly sensitive, but ease off and check with a professional if you feel sharp or worsening pain.

  1. Stand in the centre of the rebounder with your knees slightly bent
  2. Begin jogging on the spot, staying on the balls of your feet
  3. Drive each knee up toward your chest in turn
  4. Keep your chest up and pump your arms in rhythm
  5. Continue for the set time, staying centred on the mat
ea_rebounder_high_knee_runs ankleknee

Rebounder Knee Jumps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeDriving the knees up while jumping trains the hip flexors and raises the heart rate, with the mat absorbing most of the landing force. Useful for conditioning when running is off the table.

  1. Stand in the middle of the rebounder with your knees slightly bent
  2. Jump upward and pull both knees toward your chest
  3. Extend the legs again before landing
  4. Land softly in the centre of the mat with the knees bending to absorb
  5. Repeat at a controlled pace for the set time
ea_rebounder_knee_jumps ankleknee

Rebounder Knee Pushes

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeA gentler rebounder drill where the feet barely leave the mat, so it suits a warm-up or easing gradually back into impact work. Ease off or stop if you feel pain, and check with a professional if it continues. The point is rhythm, not height.

  1. Stand centred on the rebounder with a slight bend in the knees
  2. Press down into the mat rhythmically without leaving it
  3. Alternately drive one knee up as you press through the other foot
  4. Keep the movement small and controlled
  5. Continue for the set time, staying relaxed through the shoulders
ea_rebounder_knee_pushes

Rebounder Light Jumps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe simplest rebounder movement, used to warm up or to move gently on days when the body needs activity rather than training. Circulation and rhythm rather than intensity.

  1. Stand in the centre of the mat with your feet hip width apart
  2. Bounce lightly, letting your heels barely leave the surface
  3. Keep your knees soft and your shoulders relaxed
  4. Breathe steadily and stay centred on the mat
  5. Continue for the set time
ea_rebounder_light_jumps ankleknee

Rebounder in & Out From Ground

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeStepping on and off the trampoline trains the legs to accept load on two different surfaces, which challenges the ankles more than staying on one. Low impact, and it raises the heart rate quickly.

  1. Stand on the floor beside the rebounder with your knees soft
  2. Step or hop onto the mat with both feet
  3. Absorb the landing and immediately hop back off to the floor
  4. Keep your chest up and your landings quiet on both surfaces
  5. Continue at a steady rhythm for the set time
ea_rebounder_in_out_from_ground

Rebounder in & Out Jacks

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeJumping jacks on a trampoline get the heart rate up without the repeated impact through the knees that doing them on concrete produces. A sensible substitute when joints need a break.

  1. Stand in the centre of the rebounder with your feet together
  2. Jump your feet apart while raising your arms overhead
  3. Jump them back together, bringing the arms down to your sides
  4. Stay on the balls of your feet and keep the landings soft
  5. Continue at a steady pace for the set time
ea_rebounder_in_out_jacks ankleknee

Resistance Band Pull Apart

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a loop resistance band with both hands. Your arms should be extended straight in front of you at shoulder height, and your palms should be facing down
  2. Pull the resistance band apart by moving your arms out to your sides, squeezing your shoulder blades together, and keeping your arms straight
  3. Slowly return your arms to the starting position with control, maintaining tension in the band
  4. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions
ea_resistance_band_pull_apart upper_back

Resistance Band Shoulder Adduction

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Attach one end of a resistance band to a sturdy anchor point at a high height. Stand with your left side facing the anchor point, holding the other end of the band with your right hand
  2. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Extend your right arm straight out to the side parallel to the floor, palm facing down
  3. Pull the band towards your body, bringing your right hand close to your hip, keeping your arm straight
  4. Slowly return your right arm to the starting position with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then switch to the left side
ea_resistance_band_shoulder_adduction hip

Resistance Band Standing External Rotation

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and place a loop resistance band around your wrists. Keep your elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your sides, with your forearms parallel to the floor and pointing forward
  2. Rotate your shoulders outwards by pulling the resistance band apart while keeping your elbows fixed at your sides
  3. Slowly return your forearms to the starting position with control, maintaining tension in the band
  4. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions
ea_resistance_band_standing_external_rotation

Resistance Band Standing Single Arm Shoulder Extension

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Attach one end of a resistance band to a sturdy anchor point at hips height. Stand facing the anchor point and hold the other end of the band in your right hand
  2. Extend your right arm up, pointing to the anchor point, with your palm facing down
  3. Pull the band backward, keeping your arm straight, and until it reaches parallel to your side
  4. Slowly return your arm to the starting position with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then switch to the left arm
ea_resistance_band_standing_single_arm_shoulder_extension upper_back

Resistance Band Standing Single Arm Shoulder Flexion

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Attach one end of a resistance band to a sturdy anchor point at hips height. Stand with your back facing the anchor point and hold the other end of the band in your right hand
  2. Extend your right arm back, pointing to the anchor point, with your palm facing forward
  3. Pull the band forward, keeping your arm straight, and until it reaches your lower chest height
  4. Slowly return your arm to the starting position with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then switch to the left arm
ea_resistance_band_standing_single_arm_shoulder_flexion

Ring Dips

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeRings move in every direction, so the shoulders must stabilise as well as press — far harder than dips on fixed bars. Build up on parallel bars first; rings punish a shoulder that is not ready.

  1. Set the rings at about hip height and grip one in each hand
  2. Press up until your arms are straight, turning the rings out at the top
  3. Squeeze your stomach and glutes so your body stays still
  4. Lower until your shoulders are level with your elbows, keeping the rings close
  5. Press back up to a locked-out position and repeat
ea_ring_dips elbowshoulderwrist

Running

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart, your arms relaxed by your sides, and your core engaged. Maintain an upright posture
  2. Begin running by taking quick, powerful strides, lifting your knees higher than jogging
  3. Swing your arms naturally with each step, keeping them bent at a 90-degree angle
  4. Maintain a steady, comfortable pace and continue running for the desired duration or distance
ea_running ankleknee

Shadow Boxing

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly in front of the other, and your knees slightly bent. Position your hands in front of your face in a guard position, with your elbows close to your body
  2. Begin throwing punches in the air, alternating between jabs, crosses, hooks, and uppercuts. Use a full range of motion and rotate your hips and shoulders to generate power
  3. Move around as you throw your punches, incorporating footwork to simulate a real boxing match. Step forward, backward, and side to side, keeping light on your feet
  4. Continue shadow boxing for the desired duration, maintaining a steady pace and controlled movements
ea_shadow_boxing

Side to Side Punch

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand upright with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart and your knees slightly bent. Hold your fists up in front of your face in a guard position

Single Kettlebell Sled Push

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposePushing with one hand adds a strong anti-rotation demand to a leg exercise, because the load is entirely on one side. This sled-style push is a useful option when no sled is available, and trains the trunk in a way a two-handed push typically doesn't.

  1. Place a kettlebell on the floor in front of you, handle forward
  2. Get into a low athletic position with one hand on the bell
  3. Brace your stomach hard so your hips stay square
  4. Drive forward with short steps, pushing the bell along the floor
  5. Cover the set distance, then swap hands and repeat

Skater Hops

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeBounding sideways from one leg to the other trains lateral power and the ability to stick a one-leg landing, which is often when knee injuries happen. Landing quality matters more than distance -- ease off or stop if anything feels unstable or painful.

  1. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent
  2. Push off sideways and land on the opposite foot
  3. Let the free leg swing behind you as you land
  4. Absorb the landing through the hip and knee, holding your balance for a moment
  5. Push back the other way and continue for the set

Sled Battle Rope Pull

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposePulling a sled toward you hand over hand works the whole back with no lowering phase at all, so it often produces less next-day soreness than exercises with a lowering phase, letting you handle a substantial amount of volume. Grip and lungs usually run out first.

  1. Attach a rope to a loaded sled and sit or stand at the far end
  2. Take the rope in both hands and set your feet firmly
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your spine neutral
  4. Pull the rope hand over hand, drawing the sled toward you
  5. Keep pulling without pausing until the sled reaches you, then reset
ea_sled_battle_rope_pull

Sled Drag and Row

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeCombines walking with a load and a rowing pull, so legs and back work in the same set. Because nothing is lowered under load, it can be repeated often without accumulating soreness.

  1. Attach straps to the sled and hold one end in each hand
  2. Walk backwards until the straps are tight and your arms are extended
  3. Row both hands to your ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades together
  4. Extend the arms and take several steps backwards, dragging the sled
  5. Repeat the row and continue for the set distance
ea_sled_drag_and_row upper_back

  2. Simultaneously lift your right leg straight up to hip height while raising your left arm to touch your right toes

  4. Repeat the movement on the opposite side. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions

Stepmill Machine Steps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeContinuous stair climbing is one of the hardest cardiovascular efforts available at a steady pace, and it loads the glutes far more than a treadmill does. Do not lean on the handles — that removes most of the work.

  1. Step onto the machine and set a pace you can hold for the whole session
  2. Stand tall with your chest up and your hands resting lightly on the rails
  3. Place each whole foot on the step rather than just the toes
  4. Push through the whole foot (tripod foot), keeping the heel grounded, to drive yourself up onto the next step
  5. Keep the same posture for the set time — do not lean forward as you tire

Tennis Forehand Ground Stroke

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposePractising the stroke without a ball lets you rehearse the sequence — legs, hips, trunk, then arm — until it becomes automatic. The arm should be the last thing to move, not the first.

  1. Stand side-on in a ready position with your knees bent and weight balanced
  2. Turn your shoulders and take the racquet arm back as you load the back leg
  3. Drive from the back foot and rotate your hips toward the target
  4. Let the trunk turn carry the arm through the contact point
  5. Follow through across your body and return to the ready position
ea_tennis_forehand_ground_stroke

The Wall Ball

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeA squat and a throw chained together, which is why it appears in so many conditioning workouts — it exhausts the legs, shoulders and lungs at the same time. Simple to do and very hard to keep doing.

  1. Stand about half a metre from a wall holding a medicine ball at your chest
  2. Squat to about parallel, using whatever depth feels comfortable and controlled
  3. Drive up explosively and use that momentum to throw the ball at a high target on the wall
  4. Catch it as it comes down, absorbing it into the next squat
  5. Continue without stopping for the set number of repetitions
ea_the_wall_ball

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional No purpose

  2. Once you are on the moving belt, gradually increase the speed to a comfortable jogging pace, maintaining an upright posture with your core engaged
  3. Keep your arms bent at a 90-degree angle, swinging them naturally at your sides to match your jogging rhythm
  4. Maintain a steady pace, landing mid-foot with each stride and keeping your breathing steady. Jog for the desired duration or distance

  2. Once you are on the moving belt, gradually increase the speed to a running pace, maintaining an upright posture with your core engaged

Treadmill Walk

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeThe most sustainable form of training there is: enough to improve heart health and recovery, gentle enough to do every day. Adding an incline raises the effort substantially without any increase in impact.

  1. Step onto the belt and start at a slow speed before building up
  2. Stand tall with your shoulders relaxed and look ahead, not down
  3. Let your arms swing naturally rather than holding the rails
  4. Add incline rather than speed if you want the effort to go up
  5. Walk for the set time, then slow down gradually before stopping
ea_treadmill_walk

Tyre Flip

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeA full-body lift that starts as a deadlift and finishes as a press, done with an object that will not stay still. It builds strength and conditioning together, but it demands a neutral spine — start with a tyre you can clearly manage.

  1. Stand close to the tyre with your feet wide and your chest against it
  2. Squat down and get your hands under the tread with a neutral spine
  3. Drive up with your legs, keeping the tyre against your body
  4. As it rises, step in and switch your hands to push it over
  5. Push it through and reset your position before the next flip
ea_tyre_flip

Tyre Hammering

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeSwinging a hammer trains rotational power and grip endurance while raising the heart rate hard. It is one of the few conditioning exercises that improves a genuinely useful skill at the same time.

  1. Stand with the tyre in front of you and your feet shoulder width apart
  2. Hold the hammer with one hand near the head and the other at the end
  3. Raise it overhead, letting the top hand slide down toward the bottom one
  4. Swing down hard, rotating your trunk and hinging at the hips
  5. Strike the tyre, letting the head rebound under control rather than swinging free, reset, and alternate which hand leads between sets
ea_tyre_hammering

Unilateral Box Jump

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeJumping from one leg trains power on a single limb, which is how running and most sport actually happen. Use a low box — the landing is what matters, and height only adds risk here.

  1. Stand on one leg in front of a low box with the knee slightly bent
  2. Dip and swing your arms back to load the leg
  3. Jump up onto the box, landing on the same foot
  4. Absorb the landing softly with the knee tracking over the toes
  5. Step down carefully, reset, and repeat before changing legs
ea_unilateral_box_jump ankleknee

Unilateral Box Jump - Bilateral Deceleration

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional Revised

PurposeTaking off from one leg and landing on two trains the takeoff hard while making the landing easier to control. It can be a useful option if single-leg landings feel too demanding on the knee.

  1. Stand on one leg in front of a low box
  2. Dip and drive up off that single leg
  3. Land on the box with both feet at the same time
  4. Bend both knees to absorb the landing evenly
  5. Step down, reset, and alternate which leg takes off
ea_unilateral_box_jump_bilateral_deceleration ankleknee

Unilateral Front Plank

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeHolding a plank with one arm and one leg lifted takes away half your support, so the stomach has to work far harder to stop the body twisting. Ten seconds of this is worth a minute of an ordinary plank.

  1. Start in a forearm plank with your body in a straight line
  2. Squeeze your glutes and stomach and set your feet wide
  3. Lift one arm straight forward and the opposite leg off the floor
  4. Keep your hips completely level — do not let them rotate
  5. Hold for the set time, then change sides

Unilateral Jumps

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeRepeated hops on one leg build the elastic strength of the calf and the stability of the ankle, both of which running depends on. It also shows immediately which side is weaker.

  1. Stand on one leg with a slight bend in the knee
  2. Hop straight up and down on the spot, staying on the ball of the foot
  3. Keep the contacts short and the landings quiet
  4. Hold your balance without letting the free foot touch the floor
  5. Complete the set, then match the number on the other leg

Unilateral Plank

Calisthenics-Cardio-Plyo-Functional

PurposeLifting one limb from a plank halves the base of support and turns a static hold into an anti-rotation exercise. Progress by removing support rather than by holding an easy plank for longer.

  1. Set up in a plank on your forearms or hands with the feet wide
  2. Brace your stomach and squeeze your glutes
  3. Lift one foot a few centimetres off the floor
  4. Keep both hips square and level as you hold
  5. Hold for the set time, then swap to the other side

Dumbbell Decline Close Neutral Grip Press

Chest

PurposeThe decline angle points the work at the lower chest, and the close neutral grip is the kindest position there is for the front of the shoulder. A good press for anyone whose shoulders complain about the flat barbell version.

  1. Set a bench to a slight decline and hook your feet under the pads
  2. Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other and the weights touching
  3. Press them up over your lower chest until the arms are straight
  4. Lower them together toward the lower chest, keeping the elbows close to your ribs
  5. Stop when you feel a stretch across the chest, then press back up

Dumbbell Hex Press

Chest

PurposePressing the dumbbells hard against each other keeps the chest squeezing for the whole set, including at the top where a normal press goes slack. It is the easiest way to feel the inner chest working without a cable machine.

  4. Press straight up while still squeezing them together
  5. Lower slowly back to the chest without letting them come apart

Dumbbell Lying on Floor Chest Press

Chest Revised

PurposeThe floor stops your elbows before the shoulder reaches the end of its range, which limits shoulder extension compared with a bench press. If your shoulder is sore, keep the range comfortable and get it assessed rather than relying on this to fix it. It also needs no bench at all.

  1. Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, a dumbbell in each hand
  2. Press the dumbbells up over your chest until your arms are straight
  3. Lower them until the backs of your upper arms touch the floor
  4. Pause there for a moment rather than bouncing off the floor
  5. Press back up, keeping your lower back in contact with the ground

Hold the World Med Ball Chest Press

Chest

PurposeHolding a ball out in front of you loads the chest and shoulders while your stomach fights to stop you tipping back. Light in the hands and hard in the middle — a good finisher when the heavy pressing is done.

  1. Stand tall and hold a medicine ball with both hands at chest height, elbows out
  2. Squeeze the ball between your palms so the chest stays engaged
  3. Brace your stomach and keep your ribs pulled down
  4. Press the ball straight out in front of you until the arms are almost locked
  5. Hold for a moment, then draw it back to your chest without leaning back

Kettlebell Single Arm Chest Fly

Chest

PurposeOne side at a time, so the chest has to both open the arm and stop your body rolling toward the weight. That second job is what a two-handed fly never asks for, and it is why this feels harder than the load suggests.

  1. Lie on a bench with a kettlebell in one hand pressed above your chest, free hand on your stomach
  2. Keep a soft bend in the working elbow and hold it there
  3. Lower the bell out to the side in a wide arc until you feel the chest stretch
  4. Keep both shoulder blades flat on the bench — do not let your body roll
  5. Bring the bell back over your chest along the same arc, then change sides

Kneeling Push-up

Chest

PurposeA push-up with the load turned down: knees on the floor take roughly a third of your weight out of it. This is the honest way to build toward a full push-up, and far better than a full one done with a sagging back.

  1. Kneel on a mat and place your hands on the floor slightly wider than your shoulders
  2. Walk your knees back until your body makes a straight line from knees to head
  3. Squeeze your stomach and glutes so your hips do not drop
  4. Bend the elbows to lower your chest toward the floor, elbows at about forty-five degrees
  5. Push back up to straight arms without letting the hips lead

One Arm Push Up

Chest

PurposeThe hardest bodyweight press there is, and most of the difficulty is not in the chest — it is in refusing to rotate while one arm holds you up. Attempt it only when you can do clean full push-ups for reps.

  4. Bend the working elbow to lower your chest as far as you can control
  5. Press back up without twisting, then complete the set and change arms

Chest Revised

Plate Deficit Pushup

Chest

PurposeHands raised on plates let your chest travel below them, which adds the part of the range a floor push-up cuts off. That extra stretch at the bottom is where most of the new growth comes from.

  1. Place two weight plates on the floor a little wider than shoulder width
  2. Take a push-up position with one hand on each plate and your body in a straight line
  3. Brace your stomach and glutes so your hips stay level
  4. Lower until your chest drops below the level of your hands
  5. Push back up to straight arms, keeping the elbows from flaring wide
ea_plate_deficit_pushup

Plate Glute Bridge to Chest Press

Chest

PurposeTrains the two halves of the body that most people neglect together: the glutes hold the hips up while the chest presses. One plate, no bench, and both ends working at once when time is short.

  1. Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat, and hold a plate over your chest with both hands
  2. Push through your heels to lift your hips until your body is straight from knees to shoulders
  3. Hold the bridge and keep your glutes squeezed for the whole set
  4. Press the plate straight up over your chest until your arms lock
  5. Lower it back to your chest under control without letting your hips drop
ea_plate_glute_bridge_to_chest_press hipshoulder

Plate Press

Chest

PurposeSqueezing a single plate between the palms keeps the chest under tension from start to finish, including at full extension where a dumbbell press gives it a rest. Very little weight is needed for it to burn.

  1. Hold a weight plate flat between both palms at chest height, fingers pointing forward
  2. Press your hands into the plate hard enough that it cannot slip
  3. Stand tall, or lie on a bench if you prefer, with your ribs pulled down
  4. Push the plate straight away from your chest until your arms are almost straight
  5. Draw it back to your chest slowly, never stopping the inward squeeze
ea_plate_press shoulder

Push Pull Front Handle Push

Chest Revised

PurposePushing a loaded sled trains the chest, shoulders and legs together against resistance that cannot be dropped, so there is no eccentric phase and almost no next-day soreness. That makes it easy to add work without adding recovery cost.

  1. Load the sled and take the upright handles at about chest height
  2. Lean forward into the sled with your arms firm and your spine neutral
  3. Drive through the balls of your feet with short, quick steps
  4. Keep pushing at a steady pace for the set distance or time, arms straight and steady
  5. Stop, reset your breathing, then turn the sled around for the next run
ea_push_pull_front_handle_push

Kettlebell Wrist Extension

Forearms

PurposeThe opposite of the wrist curl, and the half most people skip. Balanced forearms keep the elbow quiet under heavy pressing and pulling, and this is the cheapest way to train the side that never gets worked by accident.

  2. Hold the kettlebell by the handle so it hangs below your hand
  3. Let the weight lower your knuckles toward the floor as far as is comfortable

Kettlebell Single Leg Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeTrains the hamstring and glute of one leg while your balance and your stomach work to keep you square. It transfers directly to picking things up off the floor, which is rarely done with both feet neatly planted.

  1. Stand on one leg holding a kettlebell in the opposite hand
  2. Keep a soft bend in the standing knee and lock your spine in neutral
  3. Hinge at the hip, letting the free leg extend straight behind you as a counterweight
  4. Lower until the bell is near the floor and your body forms one long line
  5. Squeeze the glute to return upright, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_kettlebell_single_leg_deadlift hiplower_back

Kettlebell Single Leg Glute Bridge

Legs

PurposeOne leg doubles the load on the glute without needing any more weight, which makes it a genuinely hard exercise you can do on a floor with one bell. It also makes a side difference impossible to miss.

  1. Lie on your back with one knee bent and that foot flat on the floor
  2. Straighten the other leg or hold that knee to your chest
  3. Rest a kettlebell on the hip of the working side and hold it in place
  4. Drive through the planted heel to lift your hips until your body is straight
  5. Lower slowly without letting your hips twist, then change legs
ea_kettlebell_single_leg_glute_bridge hip

Kettlebell Single Leg Hip Thrust

Legs

PurposeThe bench raises the shoulders for a longer range and one leg carries everything, which makes this one of the hardest glute exercises available without a barbell. Keeping the hips level is half the work.

  1. Sit with your upper back against a bench and one foot planted, knee bent
  2. Lift the other foot off the floor and hold that knee bent in the air
  3. Rest a kettlebell across the hip of the working side
  4. Drive through the planted heel until your body is straight from knee to shoulder
  5. Lower under control, keeping the hips level, then swap legs
ea_kettlebell_single_leg_hip_thrust hip

Kettlebell Single Leg Romanian Deadlifts

Legs Revised

PurposeFocuses on the hamstring through a long stretch on one leg, with a straighter knee than a single-leg deadlift. It is the version to use when the hamstring rather than the glute is what you want to load.

  1. Stand on one leg with a kettlebell in the opposite hand
  2. Keep the standing knee almost straight, with only a small give
  3. Push the hip back and lower your torso, free leg lifting behind you
  4. Keep the bell close to the standing leg and your spine neutral
  5. Stop at a deep hamstring stretch, return upright, then change sides
ea_kettlebell_single_leg_romanian_deadlifts hiplower_back

Kettlebell Split Squat

Legs No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell in each hand with your arms hanging by your sides. Take a step forward with your right foot and position your left foot back, standing on the ball of your left foot
  2. Bend both knees to lower your body into a split squat. Your back knee should hover just above the floor, and your front thigh should be parallel to the floor
  3. Push through your right heel to return to the starting position, fully extending both legs
  4. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then switch legs and perform the same number of repetitions on the other side

Kettlebell Squats

Legs No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  2. Lower your body into a squat by bending your knees and pushing your hips back as if sitting in a chair
  3. Continue lowering yourself until your thighs are parallel to the floor, making sure your knees track over your toes
  4. Push through your heels to stand back up to the starting position, fully extending your legs

Kettlebell Staggered Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeMost of the load goes through the front leg while the back foot only balances, so you get the benefit of single-leg work without needing single-leg balance. A practical way to train each side when a full one-leg version is out of reach.

  1. Stand with one foot forward and the other half a step back, that heel lifted
  2. Hold a kettlebell in each hand in front of your thighs
  3. Shift most of your weight onto the front foot
  4. Hinge at the hips and lower the bells along the front leg, spine neutral
  5. Drive through the whole front foot to stand, keeping the heel grounded, then swap the stance

Kettlebell Suitcase Squat

Legs No purpose Revised

Landmine Calf Raise

Legs Revised

PurposeLoads the calves through the shoulder rather than the hands, so grip never becomes the limit. Calves need heavy loads to grow and grip usually gives out long before they do.

  1. Load one end of a barbell in the landmine and rest it on one shoulder
  2. Stand with the balls of both feet on a plate or step, heels hanging off
  3. Hold the bar steady with the hand on that side and stand tall
  4. Let your heels drop below the step until the calves stretch
  5. Press up onto your toes as high as you can control, hold, then lower slowly
ea_landmine_calf_raise ankle

Landmine Curtsy Lunge

Legs Revised

PurposeStepping behind and across works the side of the hip, the muscle that keeps your knee tracking properly. Straight-ahead lunges never load it, which is why it stays weak in people who train legs regularly.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine with the loaded bar end at one shoulder
  2. Step one foot back and across behind the other, like a curtsy
  3. Bend both knees and lower until the back knee is near the floor
  4. Keep your hips square and your chest up throughout
  5. Push through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to return, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_landmine_curtsy_lunge hipknee

Landmine Glute Kick Back

Legs

PurposeIsolates the glute at the end of the range, where it does the work of straightening the hip. Squats and lunges load it in the stretch, so this covers the half they leave out.

  1. Stand facing the landmine and hook the loaded bar end behind one heel or ankle
  2. Hold something stable in front of you for balance
  3. Stand tall on the other leg with a soft knee
  4. Push the working leg back and up, squeezing the glute at the top
  5. Return under control without letting the back arch, then change legs
ea_landmine_glute_kick_back

Landmine Goblet Curtsy Lunge

Legs Revised

PurposeThe curtsy step loads the side of the hip, and holding the bar at the chest keeps you upright so the pattern stays clean. Better balanced than the shoulder-loaded version, and easier to learn.

  1. Stand facing away from the landmine and cup the loaded end at your chest with both hands
  2. Step one foot back and across behind the other leg
  3. Lower until both knees are bent and the back knee is near the floor
  4. Keep the chest tall and the hips facing forward
  5. Drive through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to stand, then alternate sides
ea_landmine_goblet_curtsy_lunge hipknee

Landmine Goblet Lateral Lunge

Legs

PurposeTrains stepping sideways under load, which almost no gym exercise does. It stretches the inner thigh of the straight leg and builds the hip of the bent one — both directly useful for changing direction without pulling something.

  1. Cup the loaded bar end at your chest with both hands, feet together
  2. Take a wide step directly out to one side
  3. Sit the hips back and bend that knee, keeping the other leg straight
  4. Lower until you feel the stretch along the inside of the straight leg
  5. Push off the bent leg back to the middle, then step to the other side
ea_landmine_goblet_lateral_lunge hipknee

Landmine Hack Squat

Legs Revised

PurposeThe bar's arc holds you steady, so you can sit into a deep squat with your torso upright and let the quadriceps take almost all of it. A way to train the front of the thigh hard without a squat rack.

  1. Straddle the bar with the loaded end behind you, and grip it with both hands at your sides
  2. Stand with your feet shoulder width apart and your chest up
  3. Sit straight down, keeping the torso as upright as you can
  4. Lower until your thighs are about parallel to the floor, or as far as feels comfortable and controlled
  5. Drive up through the whole foot without letting your chest tip forward
ea_landmine_hack_squat anklehipknee

Landmine Lateral Lunge

Legs

PurposeSideways movement under load, with the bar on the shoulder so the hands stay free. It builds the inner thigh and the side of the hip — the two areas that give out when you step sideways in a hurry.

  1. Rest the loaded bar end on one shoulder and stand with feet together
  2. Step wide to the side away from the loaded shoulder
  3. Push the hips back and bend that knee, other leg straight
  4. Lower until you feel a stretch on the inside of the straight leg
  5. Push back to the middle, complete the set, then load the other shoulder
ea_landmine_lateral_lunge hipknee

Landmine Lunge to Overhead Press

Legs Revised

PurposeOne movement that loads legs and shoulders in sequence, so the heart rate climbs while both get trained. Useful when the session is short and you need the whole body covered.

  1. Hold the loaded bar end at one shoulder, facing away from the anchor
  2. Step back into a reverse lunge until the back knee nearly touches the floor
  3. Drive through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to stand back up
  4. As you finish standing, press the bar up and forward to a straight arm
  5. Bring the bar back to the shoulder and repeat, alternating legs
ea_landmine_lunge_to_overhead_press hipkneeshoulder

Landmine Squat and Press

Legs

PurposeA squat that finishes as a press, so the leg drive carries into the shoulders. It teaches the whole body to work as one chain, which is what lifting anything heavy off the floor actually requires.

  1. Cup the loaded bar end at your chest with both hands, standing away from the anchor
  2. Set your feet shoulder width apart and brace your stomach
  3. Squat until your thighs are about parallel with the floor
  4. Drive up hard through your legs and let that momentum start the press
  5. Finish with the bar pressed forward and up, then bring it back to your chest
ea_landmine_squat_and_press anklehipknee

Lateral Band Walks

Legs

PurposeWakes up the muscle on the side of the hip that stops the knee collapsing inward. Doing a set of these before squatting or running noticeably changes how well the knees track.

  1. Put a loop band around your legs just above the knees or around the ankles
  2. Stand with feet hip width apart and bend into a quarter squat
  3. Keep your chest up, your toes forward and the tension on the band
  4. Step sideways with one foot, then follow with the other without letting them touch
  5. Continue for the set distance, then walk back the other way
ea_lateral_band_walks

Lateral Box Jump

Legs

PurposeJumping sideways trains power in a direction almost no training covers, and teaches the knee and hip to absorb a landing off-centre. Start with a low box — the landing matters far more than the height.

  1. Stand side-on to a low box with your feet hip width apart
  2. Dip into a quarter squat and swing your arms back
  3. Jump sideways onto the box, landing on both feet at once
  4. Land softly with your knees bent and tracking over your toes
  5. Step down carefully rather than jumping down, and reset before the next rep
ea_lateral_box_jump ankleknee

Med Ball Front Squat Raise

Legs Revised

PurposeThe ball held out in front acts as a counterweight, which lets most people squat deeper with a more upright back than they can empty-handed. A good way to open up squat depth before adding real load.

  2. Squat down as deep as you can control while keeping your chest tall
  3. At the bottom, keep your heels down and your knees tracking over your toes
  4. Stand up and, as you rise, raise the ball overhead with straight arms
  5. Lower the ball to your chest and go straight into the next squat

Medicine Ball Jumps

Legs Revised

PurposeHolding a ball while jumping adds load to the takeoff and to the landing, which builds the legs' ability to produce and absorb force quickly. Keep the sets short — this is power work, not conditioning.

  2. Dip into a quarter squat, keeping the chest up
  3. Jump straight up as high as you can control, holding the ball still
  4. Land softly on both feet with the knees bending to absorb the impact
  5. Reset to a standing position before starting the next jump

PurposeRaising the heels and narrowing the stance shifts almost everything onto the front of the thigh, and lets you stay upright through a deeper, comfortable range. This is the squat variation for building the quadriceps specifically.

  2. Hold a dumbbell vertically against your chest with both hands
  3. Keep your chest tall and your elbows tucked in
  4. Squat straight down as deep as you can control, knees travelling forward over the toes

Nordic Hamstring Curl with Partner

Legs Revised

PurposeOne of the most effective exercises for reducing hamstring injuries, which is why it is standard in football and sprint training. It loads the hamstring while it lengthens, which is exactly when tears happen.

  1. Kneel on a mat with your ankles held firmly down by a partner
  2. Keep your body straight from knees to shoulders and your stomach braced
  3. Lower your torso toward the floor as slowly as you possibly can
  4. Resist the whole way down — do not let yourself drop
  5. Catch yourself with your hands and push back up to the start

Normal Squat Smith Machine

Legs Revised

PurposeThe fixed bar path removes the balance requirement, so you can push a squat closer to failure without a spotter. It is the safer choice for training alone, at the cost of not training balance itself.

  1. Set the bar on your upper back and position your feet slightly in front of the bar
  2. Stand with feet shoulder width apart and unlock the bar
  3. Take a breath and brace your stomach
  4. Squat down until your thighs are about parallel with the floor, or as far as feels comfortable and controlled
  5. Drive up through the whole foot and re-lock the bar at the end of the set

Pistol Squat to Box

Legs

PurposeA single-leg squat with a box behind you, so the depth is set and there is somewhere to land if the leg gives out. It is how you build toward a full pistol squat without falling over learning it.

  1. Stand on one leg in front of a box or bench, the other leg extended forward
  2. Hold your arms out in front for balance
  3. Sit back and down slowly until you touch the box with your backside
  4. Do not relax onto it — keep the tension in the working leg
  5. Stand back up on the same leg, then finish the set and switch
ea_pistol_squat_to_box anklehipknee

Plate Curtsy Lunge

Legs Revised

PurposeThe crossing step loads the side of the hip, which straight lunges miss entirely. Holding a plate at the chest keeps you upright so the hips stay square and the pattern stays honest.

  1. Hold a plate against your chest with both hands, feet hip width apart
  2. Step one foot back and diagonally behind the other
  3. Bend both knees and lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor
  4. Keep your hips facing forward and your chest tall
  5. Push through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to return, alternating sides
ea_plate_curtsy_lunge hipknee

Plate Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeTeaches the deadlift pattern with a load you can hold anywhere, and the plate's narrow shape lets you keep it close to your legs. Where a barbell drifts away, this one does not let you.

  1. Stand a plate on its edge between your feet, feet hip width apart
  2. Push your hips back and bend down to grip the top of the plate with both hands
  3. Set your spine neutral, chest up and arms straight
  4. Push the floor away with your legs and stand up, keeping the plate close to your body
  5. Lower along the same path by pushing the hips back first, not by bending the back
ea_plate_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Deficit Lunge

Legs Revised

PurposeStanding on a plate lets the back knee travel below the front foot, adding range at the bottom of the lunge. That extra depth is where the glute of the front leg gets the most stretch and the most work.

  1. Stand with your front foot on a raised plate or step, holding a plate at your chest
  2. Step the other foot back and lower into a lunge
  3. Let the back knee travel below the level of the front foot
  4. Keep the front shin roughly vertical (this will vary with your anatomy) and the chest tall
  5. Push through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, to stand, then switch legs
ea_plate_deficit_lunge hipknee

Plate Forward Lunge

Legs

PurposeStepping forward loads the front of the thigh more than a reverse lunge does, and it trains the leg to absorb a step under load — which is what walking downhill and down stairs asks for.

  1. Hold a plate against your chest with both hands, standing tall
  2. Step one foot well forward and lower until both knees are near ninety degrees
  3. Let the front heel land first and keep the shin close to vertical
  4. Keep the chest up and avoid letting the front knee collapse inward
  5. Push back off the front foot to standing, then step with the other leg
ea_plate_forward_lunge hipknee

Plate Good Morning Anterior

Legs

PurposeHolding the plate out in front instead of at the chest makes the same hinge far harder on the back, because the weight sits further from your hips. Use a light plate — the leverage does the work here.

  1. Hold a light plate with straight arms out in front of your chest
  2. Stand with feet hip width apart and soften the knees
  3. Push your hips straight back and lower your chest toward the floor
  4. Keep the arms extended and the back completely flat
  5. Stop at a strong hamstring stretch, then squeeze the glutes to stand
ea_plate_good_morning_anterior hiplower_backupper_back

Plate Lateral Lunge

Legs

PurposeTrains the sideways step under load, which almost nothing else in a gym does. It stretches the inner thigh of the straight leg while loading the hip of the bent one.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest with both hands and stand with feet together
  2. Take a wide step directly out to one side
  3. Sit the hips back and bend that knee, keeping the trailing leg completely straight
  4. Lower until you feel a stretch on the inside of the straight leg
  5. Push off the bent leg to return to the middle, then step the other way
ea_plate_lateral_lunge hipknee

Plate Overhead Walking Lunge

Legs Revised

PurposeHolding a plate overhead while lunging forces the stomach and upper back to hold you upright — the moment they let go, the weight pulls you forward. It is a lunge, a shoulder hold and a brace test in one.

  1. Press a plate overhead with straight arms and keep your ribs down
  2. Step forward into a lunge until the back knee nearly touches the floor
  3. Keep the plate directly above your shoulders throughout
  4. Push through the whole foot, keeping the heel grounded, and step straight into the next lunge
  5. Continue for the set distance, keeping the arms straight the whole way
ea_plate_overhead_walking_lunge hipkneeshoulder

Plate Single Leg Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeTrains the hamstring, the glute and your balance on one leg, with a plate that stays close to the standing leg. Everyday lifting is rarely done on two evenly planted feet, and this is the version that matches it.

  1. Stand on one leg holding a plate with both hands in front of your thigh
  2. Keep a soft bend in the standing knee and lock the spine in neutral
  3. Hinge at the hip and let the free leg lift straight behind you
  4. Lower the plate along the standing leg until your body forms one line
  5. Squeeze the glute to stand tall, then finish the set and switch legs
ea_plate_single_leg_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Single Leg Pinch Grip Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeCombines a single-leg hinge with a pinch grip, so balance, hamstring and grip can each fail at different points, and you find out which one gives first. Demanding, and best kept to low repetitions.

  1. Stand on one leg with a plate on the floor beside the standing foot
  2. Pinch the plate between your fingers and thumb with the opposite hand
  3. Hinge at the hip, free leg lifting behind you, spine neutral
  4. Stand up by squeezing the glute, keeping the plate hanging still
  5. Lower it under control to the floor, then finish the set and switch sides
ea_plate_single_leg_pinch_grip_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Squat Hold

Legs

PurposeHolding the bottom of a squat under load builds the ability to stay in a position rather than move through it, which is a different quality and one that transfers to keeping your posture under fatigue.

  1. Hold a plate against your chest with both hands, feet shoulder width apart
  2. Squat down until your thighs are about parallel with the floor
  3. Keep your chest up, your heels down and your knees over your toes
  4. Hold that position for the set time, breathing normally
  5. Stand up under control rather than collapsing out of the hold
ea_plate_squat_hold anklehipknee

Plate Squat Hold Biceps Curl

Legs

PurposeCurling while holding the bottom of a squat keeps the legs under constant tension while the arms work, so a single plate covers two jobs. Efficient, and it makes the squat hold considerably harder to keep clean.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest and squat down to about parallel
  2. Hold that depth with your chest up and heels planted
  3. Extend your arms to lower the plate down in front of you
  4. Curl it back to your chest without letting your torso tip forward
  5. Continue curling for the set, then stand up out of the hold
ea_plate_squat_hold_biceps_curl anklehipknee

Plate Squat Hold Reach

Legs

PurposeReaching forward from the bottom of a squat pulls your balance toward your toes, so the legs and the stomach have to work harder to hold the position. A simple way to make a squat hold much more demanding without more weight.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest and squat down to about parallel
  2. Keep your heels flat and your chest tall in the hold
  3. Push the plate straight out in front of you until the arms are extended
  4. Hold it there without letting your heels lift or your back round
  5. Draw it back to your chest and repeat for the set
ea_plate_squat_hold_reach anklehipknee

Plate Squat Reach

Legs

PurposeAdds an arm reach to each squat, so every repetition includes a moment where the load moves away from your body and your trunk has to hold it. It turns a plain squat into a whole-body exercise.

  1. Hold a plate at your chest with both hands and stand with feet shoulder width
  2. Squat down until your thighs are about parallel with the floor
  3. At the bottom, push the plate straight out in front of you
  4. Bring it back to your chest before you start standing
  5. Stand up fully and repeat for the set
ea_plate_squat_reach anklehipknee

Plate Staggered Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeMost of the weight goes through the front leg while the back foot only steadies you, so each side gets trained without needing single-leg balance. The practical way to even out a stronger and weaker leg.

  1. Stand with one foot forward and the other half a step back with the heel raised
  2. Hold a plate with both hands in front of your thighs
  3. Put about eighty percent of your weight on the front foot
  4. Hinge at the hips and lower the plate along the front leg with a neutral spine
  5. Drive through the whole front foot (tripod foot) while keeping the heel grounded to stand, then swap the stance
ea_plate_staggered_deadlift hiplower_back

Plate Staggered Pinch Grip Deadlift

Legs Revised

PurposeThe staggered stance loads one leg while the pinch grip loads the fingers, so this trains the hinge and the grip in the same set. Grip usually fails first, which makes it a natural way to cap the load.

  1. Stand with one foot forward and the other half a step back, heel raised
  2. Pinch a plate in each hand by the smooth outer face, arms hanging
  3. Shift most of your weight onto the front foot
  4. Hinge at the hips and lower the plates along the front leg, spine neutral
  5. Stand back up through the front heel, then change the stance
ea_plate_staggered_pinch_grip_deadlift hiplower_back

Barbell Hang Clean

Powerlifting Revised

PurposeTeaches the body to produce force fast rather than merely to lift a lot. Starting from the hang removes the floor pull, so the whole exercise is the hip snap — the same explosive extension behind a jump, a sprint start and a throw.

  1. Stand holding the bar at arm's length, hands just outside the hips, feet hip-width
  2. Push the hips back and slide the bar down the thighs to just above the knee, spine neutral, chest up
  3. Drive the hips forward hard and shrug — the bar is thrown upward by the legs, not pulled by the arms
  4. As it rises, drop under it and spin the elbows through to catch the bar on the front of the shoulders
  5. Stand up out of the catch, then lower the bar back to the hang and reset before the next rep
ea_barbell_hang_clean lower_backwrist

Barbell Press Under

Powerlifting

PurposeDrills the second half of a clean or snatch — the moment you stop pushing the bar up and start pushing yourself down under it. Most missed lifts are not a weak pull, they are a slow turnover, and this is how that gets faster.

  1. Hold the bar at the front of the shoulders with a light load — this is a technique drill, not a strength lift
  2. Keep the bar path vertical and the torso upright throughout
  3. Press yourself DOWN under the bar rather than pressing the bar up, dropping into a quarter squat
  4. Lock the arms overhead at the same moment your hips stop descending
  5. Stand up under control and reset; add weight only once the two happen together
ea_barbell_press_under kneeshoulder

Plate Clean

Powerlifting Revised

PurposeThe hip drive of a barbell clean with none of its technical cost. A plate is easier to hold, easier to bail, and lets you rehearse the explosive extension long before a loaded bar is a sensible idea.

  1. Stand with the plate on the floor between your feet, held at its sides with both hands
  2. Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine and grip the plate low
  3. Drive through the floor and extend the hips hard, letting the plate float upward
  4. Pull yourself under it and catch it at chest height with the elbows up
  5. Lower it back to the floor under control rather than dropping it
ea_plate_clean lower_backwrist

Plate Clean and Press

Powerlifting

PurposeOne movement from the floor to overhead, so legs, trunk and shoulders have to hand the load off to each other without a pause. That handover is what makes it a conditioning exercise as much as a strength one.

  1. Start with the plate on the floor between your feet, gripped at the sides
  2. Hinge, then extend the hips explosively and catch the plate at chest height
  3. Without resetting, brace the trunk and press the plate straight overhead
  4. Keep the ribs down — the lower back should not arch to finish the press
  5. Return the plate to the chest, then to the floor, and repeat
ea_plate_clean_and_press kneelower_backshoulderwrist

Plate Thruster

Powerlifting Revised

PurposeA front squat and an overhead press joined into one rep, which is why it raises the heart rate faster than either alone. The legs finish the squat and the arms start the press at the same instant — that overlap is the whole point.

  1. Hold the plate at chest height with both hands, feet shoulder-width
  2. Squat down as deep as you can control while keeping the chest tall and the heels down
  3. Stand up out of the squat and, without pausing, use that momentum to press the plate overhead
  4. Extend the arms fully with the plate over the middle of your feet, without forcing the elbows
  5. Bring it back to the chest as you descend into the next rep
ea_plate_thruster

Sandbag Cleans

Powerlifting Revised

PurposeA clean with a load that shifts while you lift it. The sand moves, so the trunk has to correct continuously — closer to carrying a person or a piece of furniture than any barbell lift will ever be.

  1. Stand over the bag with feet hip-width and grip it by the handles or hug it at the sides
  2. Hinge at the hips, keep the spine neutral, and pull the bag to the top of the thighs
  3. Extend the hips hard and pull the bag up the body, keeping it in contact
  4. Drop the elbows under and catch it high on the chest, hugging it tight
  5. Lower it to the floor under control — resist the urge to let it drop and yank your back
ea_sandbag_cleans lower_backwrist

PurposeLying on an incline changes the direction of the load, so the shrug pulls the shoulder blades down and back instead of straight up. That is the direction that helps posture rather than the one that builds a thicker neck.

Dumbbell Plank Pullthrough

Shoulders

PurposeReaching under your body to drag a weight while holding a plank forces the shoulder that stays down to hold the whole load, and the stomach to stop the hips rotating. Two jobs at once, and neither can be faked.

  1. Set up in a high plank with a dumbbell on the floor just outside one hand
  2. Widen your feet for balance and squeeze your glutes and stomach
  3. Reach under your chest with the opposite hand and grip the dumbbell
  4. Drag it across to the other side while keeping your hips completely level
  5. Return that hand to the floor and repeat, alternating sides

Dumbbell Shoulder Extension

Shoulders Revised

PurposeTaking the arms behind the body works the back of the shoulder and the lats through a range that many other shoulder movements do not reach. It also stretches the front of the shoulders as the arms travel back.

  2. Keep the ribs down and the chest open, without arching the lower back
  3. Sweep both arms straight back behind you with the elbows straight
  4. Go only as far as the shoulders allow without the chest collapsing forward
  5. Return to your sides slowly, resisting the weight the whole way

PurposeBuilds the side of the shoulder and the upper trapezius together. Using one arm lets the elbow travel on the path your own shoulder prefers, which some people find more comfortable than the two-handed barbell version.

Cocoons

Stretching - Mobility No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Begin by lying flat on your back with your legs extended straight and your arms extended overhead on the floor
  2. Engage your core and simultaneously lift your legs off the floor while bringing your arms forward to meet your knees, curling your body into a "cocoon" position
  3. Hold the cocoon position for a moment, squeezing your core muscles

Corner Wall Chest Stretch

Stretching - Mobility No purpose

Purposenot written yet (H3 pending)

  1. Begin by standing in front of a corner of a wall with your feet shoulder-width apart. Place your palms flat against the walls at your sides, with your elbows slightly below shoulder height
  2. Lean forward into the corner, keeping your legs in place, to lean into the stretch
  3. Push your chest forward towards the corner, feeling the stretch across your chest and shoulders. Hold this position for the desired duration
